amendments.rule: An English particle or adverb that realizes a Greek **preverb** rides inside the compound verb's own unit and is never `added`, as a discontinuous realization under rule 15 where the ASV separates them: `ἐξῆλθεν` → *went forth*, `ἐξέβαλον` → *cast out*, `ἀνέβη` → *went up*, `ἐπεβίβασαν` → *set thereon* at LUK.19.35, `προσηργάσατο` → *hath made more* at LUK.19.16, `ἀπολάβωσιν` → *receive again* at LUK.6.34. The head is the English word glossing the **verbal root**, never the particle. The corpus is unanimous: 963 units across 141 chapters carry such a particle and every one of them is `aligned`, none `added`, and the head stands on the verb word in all but one class. This is scoped to a particle **no other source token stands to answer to**. Where an expressed preposition does answer to it — because the particle is part of that preposition's own English gloss, as *out* is of `ἐκ` → *out of* — the whole English prepositional expression is the preposition's, headed on the prepositional word, and the compound verb keeps only its verb word: `ἔξελθε ἐξ αὐτοῦ` → *come* and *out of*, `ἐξῆλθεν ἐξ αὐτοῦ` → *came* and *out of*, as `εἰσελθὼν εἰς` → *entered* and *into* and `ἀπῆλθεν ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ` → *departed* and *from* do. Rule 36 is what decides that and says it in terms: an English preposition governing a prepositional phrase realizes the Greek preposition and not the verb it depends on, even where English idiom makes the verb phrasal, and a preposition is left `unrepresented` only where English realizes it nowhere at all — so do not leave such a preposition a bare *of* while the verb takes the *out*. That arm is scoped to where the ASV writes **one** English particle for the two, and the count of English words the ASV wrote is what decides it, as rule 94 decides a compound unit by that same test. Where the ASV writes a particle for the preverb **in addition to** a complete prepositional expression, each token takes its own and the verb does not go bare: `Ἔξελθε … ἐκ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου` → *Come forth* and *out of the man* gives *forth* to the imperative and *out of* to `ἐκ`, as `τὴν ἐξ αὐτοῦ δύναμιν ἐξελθοῦσαν` → *the power proceeding from him had gone forth* gives *forth* to the participle and *proceeding from* to `ἐξ`. That the preverb and the preposition are the same morpheme is not the test and does not strand the extra word: this rule's own count forbids marking such a particle `added`, and rule 36 forbids handing it to a preposition whose English is already complete, so the verb is the only token left to take it. A **noncompositional prepositional phrase** standing in the same clause answers to the particle in the same way, and the single English word is that phrase's rather than the preverb's: `συνήχθησαν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό` → *were gathered together* gives *were gathered* to the verb and *together* to `ἐπί` + `αὐτό` as one `noncompositional` unit under rule 45, the intervening article standing `unrepresented` under rule 93, as MAT.22.34 and ACT.4.26 read it and as ACT.2.44 reads the same phrase where no compound verb competes. Where no such phrase stands, the preverb keeps the word in the ordinary way, which is why `συνηγμένοι` → *gathered together* and `συνήχθησαν` → *were gathered together* keep *together* inside the verb's own unit. A preverb whose sense the following preposition's gloss does **not** carry keeps this rule's ordinary treatment, which is why `ἀναβαίνων ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος` → *coming up out of the water* gives *up* to the participle and *out of* to `ἐκ` in one clause, and why `ἐκβάλλει … εἰς` → *driveth … forth* and *into* does. Rule 94 decides only whether the preposition and the word it governs form one unit, and does not decide where the particle goes. Where the compound verb governs a bare dative or genitive that the ASV writes with an English preposition, that preposition realizes the case government and rides with the governed word under rules 21, 36 and 69, as MRK.14.65 has it and as ACT.4.1 `ἐπέστησαν αὐτοῖς` → *came* and *upon them* and ACT.4.3 `ἐπέβαλον … αὐτοῖς` → *laid* and *on them* do. That arm too is scoped to where the ASV writes an English **verb word of its own** for the compound, as *came* and *laid* are. Where it writes none, and the English preposition is the only word carrying the compound's lexical sense, the preposition stays inside the verb's unit and the governed word takes its bare pronoun or noun: `προϊσταμένους ὑμῶν` → *are over* and *you* gives *are over* to the participle headed on *over* and a bare *you* to the genitive, `προΐστημι` meaning to stand before while *are* is only the periphrastic copula. Rule 17 is what forces this, forbidding a head on a subject or an auxiliary: a unit stripped to *are* would have no lexical word left to head on, whereas the governed word loses nothing, its case being what the verb's own sense already expresses. 1TH.5 writes both arms, giving *upon them* to the dative of `ἐφίσταται` → *cometh upon them* and keeping *over* with the participle of `προϊσταμένους`, which is what shows that an English verb word standing for the compound, and not which oblique case the verb governs, is what decides between those two. An **accusative** object is the contrast, and there the case is exactly what decides: English writes no preposition to realize an accusative, so where the ASV gives such an object an English preposition that preposition is the verb's own phrasal government and stays inside the verb's unit, the governed word keeping a bare noun or pronoun. `ἐκδεχομένου αὐτούς` → *waited for them* gives *waited for* to the participle and a bare *them* to the pronoun, as `ψηλαφήσειαν αὐτόν` → *feel after him* gives *feel after* to the optative and `ἀκούσαντες ἀνάστασιν` → *heard of the resurrection* gives *heard of* to the participle. Rules 21 and 36 are why: rule 21 hands a governed word the English preposition that realizes its **case**, and an accusative has none to realize, while rule 36 leaves a preposition with the verb only where no Greek preposition is expressed for it to answer to, which is exactly this configuration. ACT.17 writes both arms, giving *with them*, *with Paul*, *of him* and *unto him* to the oblique objects of `διαλέγομαι`, `προσκληρόομαι`, `ἐπιλαμβάνομαι` and `κολλάομαι` and keeping *for*, *after* and *of* inside the verbs of `ἐκδέχομαι`, `ψηλαφάω` and `ἀκούω`. Where a Greek preposition **is** expressed the question does not arise and rule 36 gives it the English word, as it does for `ἀκούω` with `περί` → *hear of your state*. That expressed preposition need not govern the object itself, and the object's own case does not shield it: where the accusative object is a **substantival article** whose phrase an expressed preposition governs, the English preposition standing between the verb and that phrase answers to the Greek preposition and never to the verb, the article keeping only the nominal the ASV writes for it and the verb going bare. `διαγινώσκειν … τὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ` → *judge of his case* gives a bare *judge* to the verb, *of* to `περί`, *his* to `αὐτοῦ` and *case* to the article, exactly as rule 36's `τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν … μεριμνήσει` → *will care truly for your state* gives *for* to `περί` and *will care* to the verb. Rule 36's compression clause is the contrast and is narrow: it empties `περί` only where the ASV writes no preposition at all, as `τὰ περὶ ἡμῶν` → *our state* does. So ask what stands **inside** the object phrase before reading an English preposition as the verb's, and do not read a phrasal English verb as evidence that its particle belongs to the object: the test is whether the object's own case is a case English realizes with a preposition **and** whether its phrase carries a preposition of its own, which is why `ἀκούσαντες ἀνάστασιν` → *heard of the resurrection* is this arm's case and the same verb with a `περί` phrase for its object is not. The one exception is an idiom that leaves no English verb word to head on at all: `Ἆρον` → *away with him* at JHN.19.15 and `Αἶρε` → *away with* at LUK.23.18 head on *away*, because nothing else was written.
amendments.why: ACT.23.15 `διαγινώσκειν … τὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ` → *judge of his case* was aligned by giving *of* to the verb and leaving `περί` `unrepresented`. The pass reached that by reading the accusative arm's sentence — 'a preposition standing over an accusative object is the verb's or the frame's and never the object's' — off the case of the object token `τά`, without noticing that the expressed `περί` governs a genitive inside that object's own phrase. The rule already deferred to rule 36 'where a Greek preposition is expressed', but did not say where it must be expressed, and the accusative arm's own summary test ('whether the object's own case is a case English realizes with a preposition') returns the wrong answer for this configuration on its face. The amendment states the scope and gives the shape, and it contradicts nothing: rule 36's own cited example `τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν … μεριμνήσει` → *for your state* is this exact construction decided this exact way, and `ἀκούω` with `περί` → *hear of your state* is already named in rule 106's own text. The chapter reads it the amended way at 23.11, 23.20 and 23.34 and the outlier at 23.15 is patched above. The final sentence of the accusative arm is widened rather than left standing, so a later reader meets the qualification where the over-broad test is, not in a cross-reference.

conventions: Ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί → Brethren: the ASV writes one English word for the pair and it is ἀδελφοί's, ἀδελφοί alone carrying it. Ἄνδρες is its own unrepresented unit and is not joined to the noun (ACT.23.1, ACT.23.6).

ἕως οὗ → till and until is one aligned unit taking the single English word, headed on ἕως, as rule 50 reads ἕως ἄν → till. The relative genitive is not left unrepresented and the one word is not split across the pair (ACT.23.12, ACT.23.14, ACT.23.21).

Where the ASV writes one English word for μὲν οὖν it is So, and it is οὖν's under rule 70's operational test, μέν standing unrepresented (ACT.23.18, ACT.23.22, ACT.23.31). A μέν with no οὖν beside it and no word of its own is empty for the same reason (ACT.23.8).

Recurring lexical heads in this chapter: χιλίαρχος → chief captain heads on captain, as ἀρχιερεύς → high priest heads on priest (rule 66), and not on chief; νεανίας and νεανίσκος → young man head on young, man being the generic completion; ἀναθεματίζω → bound under a curse heads on curse, the verb being denominal from ἀνάθεμα while bound glosses no element of it; ἐνέδρα → lying in wait and ἐνεδρεύω → lie in wait for both head on wait.

τὰ περὶ + genitive, and an expressed preposition generally: where the ASV writes an English preposition for the phrase it belongs to the Greek preposition and not to the governing verb, even where the verb reads as phrasal and its object is the accusative article — judge of his case (ACT.23.15), inquire concerning him (ACT.23.20), testified concerning me (ACT.23.11), asked of what province on ἐκ (ACT.23.34). Rule 106's accusative arm reaches only an object with no preposition of its own, as heard of the ambush does at ACT.23.16; περί is unrepresented only where the ASV compresses the phrase into a bare possessive and writes no preposition at all.

report: Read all 69 candidate lemma groups and then the full dump end to end, since the table is blind to `added` units (this chapter has one, ACT.23.24's supplied *he bade them*). One real split found.

SPLIT — `τὰ περὶ` + genitive under a phrasal English verb. ACT.23.11 gives *concerning* to `περί`, ACT.23.20 gives *concerning* to `περί`, and ACT.23.34 gives *of* to `ἐκ` though *asked of* reads phrasal; ACT.23.15 alone left `περί` `unrepresented` and handed *of* to `διαγινώσκειν` under rule 106's accusative arm. Nothing in the source licenses the difference: rule 106 defers in terms to rule 36 wherever a Greek preposition is expressed, and rule 36's own `τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν … μεριμνήσει` → *for your state* is this exact shape. Patched ACT.23.15 — *of* to `περί`, a bare *judge* to the verb. The pass read the object's case (accusative `τά`) and missed that the expressed `περί` stands inside the object phrase; rule 106 is amended below to close that reading.

BSB — ten disagreements, one genuine (ACT.23.15 `περί`, patched). The other nine are documented convention differences and none is an error: rule 20 displacement at 23.4 (*God's*), 23.5 (*thy*), 23.16 (*sister's*), 23.29 (*their*); rule 57's inner and outer article at 23.9; rule 61's nominalizing article at 23.15; rule 23 before a name at 23.10; rule 70 `μέν` at 23.8; rule 65's unwritten `καί` at 23.34. No accepted edge was touched to move the rate.

Checked and consistent: preverb against expressed preposition (23.16 and 23.33 leave the verb bare and give the preposition its word, while 23.10, 23.15, 23.20 and 23.28 keep *down* inside the verb, `κατα-` being a sense *unto* does not carry); oblique government (`παρίστημι` and `ἐφίστημι` with a bare dative put the preposition on the dative at 23.2, 23.11 and 23.33, on the preverb where no dative stands at 23.4 and 23.27, and on the article at 23.19, `ἐπιλαμβάνομαι` + genitive → *by the*); accusative government (*smite … on*, *speak … of*, *heard of*, *lie in wait for*, *looking for*).

Also checked and consistent: rule 88 junctures in sixteen verses, every one on the verb of the clause it introduces; rule 74 supplied objects and participial subjects throughout; articles before names; `μὲν οὖν` at 23.18, 23.22, 23.31; `τε` at 23.5, 23.10, 23.24, 23.28; `ἕως οὗ` at 23.12, 23.14, 23.21; `ὅπως` at 23.15, 23.20, 23.23 (rule 24 — one analysis, two ASV renderings); recitative `ὅτι` at 23.5 and 23.20 against complementizer `ὅτι` elsewhere; `ἀναθεματίζω` at 23.12, 23.14 and 23.21, where 23.14's expressed `Ἀναθέματι` is what leaves the verb a bare *bound*; `ποιέω` + noun collapsed at 23.12 and split at 23.13, which the ASV's own wording licenses under rule 73.

Note defect, not patched: ACT.23.6's unit for `ἔκραζεν` → *cried out* cites rule 106's preverb, but `κράζω` carries no preverb and *out* is simply part of the English rendering, with no other token to answer to it. The edge is right and unchanged, so I did not re-emit the verse; drop the citation when 23.6 is next touched.

Conventions: the log had 0 entries against 27 repeated notes. Five chapter-wide judgments are now recorded — the ones a later reader could not derive from the contract alone. The remaining repetitions restate rules 20, 23, 32, 38, 40, 51, 61, 65, 70, 74, 88 and 106 and are left unlogged deliberately.
